content:
I have some preliminary results extending the formalization work done on Erdos 690, adapting the Wang-Crapis paper, which proves non-unimodality for all k > 3 by proving a reversal exists for finite k < 38001 and an analytic argument covering k >= 38001. This project, available at https://github.com/kimihiro64/prime-factor-oscillations, goes further and establishes a double exponential growth rate of those reversals as k grows before a final descent (as well as some small exploration of how it behaves for affine sums). It also shows that the exact rate is dependent on prime gap frequencies, with a converse argument showing that sufficiently late ascents for all k imply infinitely many prime gaps of width H. The associated constant in the growth rate is 1/(H+1) for ordinary integers, which gives the unconditional eventual bound of 1/3 since we can't have infinite prime gaps lower than 2. Experimentally, I used some tricks to scan for latest ascents and was able to feasibly check through k = 50 on my laptop, there is a small crossing above 1/3 at k = 12, but after that it drops below and steadily approaches 1/3 from below. There are also some conditional results showing what kinds of gaps can be the latest ascent, under Hardy-Littlewood conjecture on twin prime density (and maybe some slightly weaker results), it will always be a twin prime gap eventually.

It's still in progress research and I haven't done too many passes over the quality of the paper or set up the CI yet to make actual release builds, but the Lean code does build locally. I've been looking into ways to independently establish late ascents as a means of lowering the bounded prime gap record from 186, but currently all such attempts have been blocked by insufficiently powerful sieve estimates or invalid conditions to apply estimates with given techniques. Small prime residue conditions control the bulk of the mass near exactly, but the remaining terms to be estimated are semiprimes over the cube root scale. There may be a route through Friedlander-Iwaniec if the necessary bilinear cancellation estimate could be derived for this case, although it doesn't seem clear that it can be.

Without an actual way to lower the bounded prime gap record, I'm not sure how publishable this result is, but it seems interesting none the less. It connects natural density of prime factors, multiplicative information, to additive information in prime gaps.

I do have an idea to maybe bypass it, although I'm out of codex usage for a few days and can only bounce ideas off of ChatGPT Pro. But we did prove that the bounded gap relation doesn't just apply to the normal integers, it also applies to the odd only integers. Supposedly, it should also apply to many different families, like 2p+1, basically any family with a local law spectrum obeying

ηℓ−1=ℓν+β+o(1)\eta_\ell^{-1}=\frac{\ell}{\nu}+\beta+o(1)ηℓ−1​=νℓ​+β+o(1)

I'm not sure if this could also be extended to non-linear families, but potentially the idea is you pick one that has enough structure that we actually can do proper sieve estimates with the strength required to force sufficiently late ascents for the restricted family, which of course would imply infinitely many such bounded gaps in both that family and the integers. In my mind it seems kind of intuitive because the ascents are going to happen regardless of what family it filters through so long as they're not /too/ restricted, but the information we need to force ascents is reduced (maybe). I'll look into it more thoroughly when codex usage comes back.

It's not fully solved yet, but there is a way to change the family to a^2 +2b^4, restricted to odd square-free outputs, which lets us take advantage of the less parity-sensitive Friedlander-Iwaniec sieve type methods thanks to a result from Xiao in 2024. Theoretically it can take bounded prime gaps all the way down to 2, and going lower in some senses reduces the math involved because it lowers the number of density ranks that need to be considered, at the cost of a harder signed lower bound to prove at the end. Pushed a rough draft of the argument to the repo, but the bound itself may not be in reach. Certainly not by ChatGPT pro
